claim: Modern high efficacy disease modifying therapies have revolutionized the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
source: While modern high efficacy disease modifying therapies have revolutionized the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, they are less effective at controlling progressive forms of the disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical impact of disease modifying therapies, drawing from established medical knowledge and consensus in the field of multiple sclerosis treatment.

claim: Disease modifying therapies are less effective at controlling progressive forms of multiple sclerosis.
source: While modern high efficacy disease modifying therapies have revolutionized the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, they are less effective at controlling progressive forms of the disease.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical knowledge about the differential efficacy of disease modifying therapies across MS subtypes.

claim: Meningeal inflammation is a recognized risk factor for cortical gray matter pathology.
source: Meningeal inflammation is a recognized risk factor for cortical gray matter pathology which can result in disabling symptoms such as cognitive impairment and depression, but the mechanisms linking meningeal inflammation and gray matter pathology remain unclear.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Cortical gray matter pathology can result in disabling symptoms such as cognitive impairment and depression.
source: Meningeal inflammation is a recognized risk factor for cortical gray matter pathology which can result in disabling symptoms such as cognitive impairment and depression, but the mechanisms linking meningeal inflammation and gray matter pathology remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by established clinical knowledge about the consequences of gray matter pathology in MS.

claim: The mechanisms linking meningeal inflammation and gray matter pathology remain unclear.
source: Meningeal inflammation is a recognized risk factor for cortical gray matter pathology which can result in disabling symptoms such as cognitive impairment and depression, but the mechanisms linking meningeal inflammation and gray matter pathology remain unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field, which is the motivation for the current study.

claim: MRI-guided spatial transcriptomics was performed in a mouse model of autoimmune meningeal inflammation.
source: Here, we performed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided spatial transcriptomics in a mouse model of autoimmune meningeal inflammation to characterize the transcriptional signature in areas of meningeal inflammation and the underlying brain parenchyma.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, which is detailed in the methods and results sections.

claim: Inflammatory signaling pathways are broadly increased at sites of meningeal inflammation.
source: We found broadly increased activity of inflammatory signaling pathways at sites of meningeal inflammation, but only a subset of these pathways active in the adjacent brain parenchyma.
evidence: This finding is supported by the PROGENy pathway analysis and gene expression data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Only a subset of inflammatory pathways active in meningeal inflammation are active in the adjacent brain parenchyma.
source: We found broadly increased activity of inflammatory signaling pathways at sites of meningeal inflammation, but only a subset of these pathways active in the adjacent brain parenchyma.
evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis and trajectory modeling showing differential pathway activity.

claim: Complement signaling is induced in brain parenchyma adjacent to meningeal inflammation.
source: Subclustering of regions adjacent to meningeal inflammation revealed the subset of immune programs induced in brain parenchyma, notably complement signaling and antigen processing/presentation.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Antigen processing/presentation is induced in brain parenchyma adjacent to meningeal inflammation.
source: Subclustering of regions adjacent to meningeal inflammation revealed the subset of immune programs induced in brain parenchyma, notably complement signaling and antigen processing/presentation.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Immune signatures originating from meningeal inflammation show variable penetration into adjacent brain tissue.
source: Trajectory gene and gene set modeling analysis confirmed variable penetration of immune signatures originating from meningeal inflammation into the adjacent brain tissue.
evidence: This is supported by the trajectory analysis presented in Figure 5 and validated by RNAscope.

claim: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system characterized by a relapsing remitting and/or progressive course of demyelination, axonal injury, and neurologic dysfunction.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) characterized by a relapsing remitting and/or progressive course of demyelination, axonal injury, and neurologic dysfunction (Reich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about MS supported by a citation to Reich et al., 2018.

claim: Highly efficacious disease modifying therapies have revolutionized the prevention and treatment of MS relapses.
source: Highly efficacious disease modifying therapies have revolutionized the prevention and treatment of MS relapses, but are less effective at stopping hallmarks of MS progression such as brain atrophy (Faissner et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Faissner et al., 2019 and reflects established clinical knowledge.

claim: Disease modifying therapies are less effective at stopping hallmarks of MS progression such as brain atrophy.
source: Highly efficacious disease modifying therapies have revolutionized the prevention and treatment of MS relapses, but are less effective at stopping hallmarks of MS progression such as brain atrophy (Faissner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Faissner et al., 2019.

claim: Leptomeningeal inflammation plays a pivotal role in contributing to MS pathology.
source: Accumulating evidence points to a pivotal role for leptomeningeal inflammation (LMI) in contributing to this pathology (Howell et al., 2011; Absinta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Howell et al., 2011 and Absinta et al., 2015.

claim: Leptomeningeal inflammation is found in all subtypes of MS.
source: LMI is found in all subtypes of MS, ranging histologically from disorganized collections of leukocytes to highly organized ectopic lymphoid follicles, and correlates with the presence of cortical gray matter demyelination, neurite loss, and decreased volume (Wicken et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wicken et al., 2018.

claim: Leptomeningeal inflammation ranges histologically from disorganized collections of leukocytes to highly organized ectopic lymphoid follicles.
source: LMI is found in all subtypes of MS, ranging histologically from disorganized collections of leukocytes to highly organized ectopic lymphoid follicles, and correlates with the presence of cortical gray matter demyelination, neurite loss, and decreased volume (Wicken et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wicken et al., 2018.

claim: Leptomeningeal inflammation correlates with the presence of cortical gray matter demyelination, neurite loss, and decreased volume.
source: LMI is found in all subtypes of MS, ranging histologically from disorganized collections of leukocytes to highly organized ectopic lymphoid follicles, and correlates with the presence of cortical gray matter demyelination, neurite loss, and decreased volume (Wicken et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wicken et al., 2018.

claim: Gray matter pathology has been linked to debilitating symptoms such as cognitive impairment and depression.
source: Gray matter pathology (GMP) has been linked to debilitating symptoms such as cognitive impairment and depression (Geurts and Barkhof, 2008), and tends to occur in spatial relation to areas of LMI.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Geurts and Barkhof, 2008.

claim: Gray matter pathology tends to occur in spatial relation to areas of leptomeningeal inflammation.
source: Gray matter pathology (GMP) has been linked to debilitating symptoms such as cognitive impairment and depression (Geurts and Barkhof, 2008), and tends to occur in spatial relation to areas of LMI.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Geurts and Barkhof, 2008 and is a key observation motivating the study.

claim: The most common gray matter lesion location is directly sub-pial.
source: Indeed, the most common gray matter lesion location is directly sub-pial (Bø et al., 2003a), and there is a gradient of increased pathology toward the surface of the brain in MS patients (Magliozzi et al., 2010; Mainero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bø et al., 2003a.

claim: There is a gradient of increased pathology toward the surface of the brain in MS patients.
source: Indeed, the most common gray matter lesion location is directly sub-pial (Bø et al., 2003a), and there is a gradient of increased pathology toward the surface of the brain in MS patients (Magliozzi et al., 2010; Mainero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Magliozzi et al., 2010 and Mainero et al., 2015.

claim: Gray matter pathology occurs without local blood-brain barrier disruption.
source: Interestingly, GMP occurs without local blood-brain barrier disruption or robust infiltration of peripheral immune cells into the brain parenchyma (van Horssen et al., 2007; Bø et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Horssen et al., 2007 and Bø et al., 2003b.

claim: Gray matter pathology occurs without robust infiltration of peripheral immune cells into the brain parenchyma.
source: Interestingly, GMP occurs without local blood-brain barrier disruption or robust infiltration of peripheral immune cells into the brain parenchyma (van Horssen et al., 2007; Bø et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Horssen et al., 2007 and Bø et al., 2003b.

claim: Leptomeningeal inflammation is speculated to be a source of pro-inflammatory molecules that contribute to gray matter pathology.
source: LMI is therefore speculated to be a source of pro-inflammatory molecules that contribute to GMP (Pikor et al., 2015), but the pathway(s) involved remain(s) unknown.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Pikor et al., 2015.

claim: The pathways by which leptomeningeal inflammation contributes to gray matter pathology remain unknown.
source: LMI is therefore speculated to be a source of pro-inflammatory molecules that contribute to GMP (Pikor et al., 2015), but the pathway(s) involved remain(s) unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: Magliozzi and colleagues identified increased expression of numerous cytokines and chemokines in the meninges and CSF of post-mortem MS cases with high levels of meningeal inflammation and GM demyelination.
source: Magliozzi and colleagues identified increased expression of numerous cytokines and chemokines, including interferon gamma (IFNγ), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), interleukin (IL)-2, IL-22, CXCL13, and CXCL10, in the meninges and CSF of post-mortem MS cases with high levels of meningeal inflammation and GM demyelination (Magliozzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magliozzi et al., 2018.

claim: Interferon gamma, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-2, IL-22, CXCL13, and CXCL10 are increased in the meninges and CSF of post-mortem MS cases with high levels of meningeal inflammation and GM demyelination.
source: Magliozzi and colleagues identified increased expression of numerous cytokines and chemokines, including interferon gamma (IFNγ), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), interleukin (IL)-2, IL-22, CXCL13, and CXCL10, in the meninges and CSF of post-mortem MS cases with high levels of meningeal inflammation and GM demyelination (Magliozzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magliozzi et al., 2018.

claim: Microarray analysis of cortical lesions from MS cases with LMI revealed a shift in TNF signaling from TNFR1/TNFR2-mediated anti-apoptotic pathways toward TNFR1- and RIPK3-mediated pro-apoptotic/pro-necroptotic pathways.
source: Microarray analysis of cortical lesions from MS cases with LMI revealed a shift in TNF signaling from TNFR1/TNFR2 and I-mediated anti-apoptotic pathways toward TNFR1- and RIPK3-mediated pro-apoptotic/pro-necroptotic pathways (Magliozzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magliozzi et al., 2019.

claim: Sub-pial cortical lesions in marmoset and rat models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis were found with prominent microglial activation and immunoglobulin deposition on myelin sheaths.
source: In marmoset and rat models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), sub-pial cortical lesions were found with prominent microglial activation and immunoglobulin deposition on myelin sheaths (Storch et al., 2006; Merkler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Storch et al., 2006 and Merkler et al., 2006.

claim: Complement deposition is not found in purely cortical gray matter lesions, in contrast to white or gray/white matter lesions.
source: Interestingly, complement deposition, one possible mechanism of immunoglobulin-related cellular injury, is not found in purely cortical gray matter lesions, in contrast to white or gray/white matter lesions (Brink et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brink et al., 2005.

claim: Previous attempts to characterize the relation between LMI and GMP have been limited by the absence of spatially resolved data.
source: Previous attempts to characterize the relation between LMI and GMP have been limited by the absence of spatially resolved data, which therefore lacks critical information about the anatomic relationship between LMI and the underlying brain parenchyma.
evidence: This identifies a methodological limitation in prior studies that the current work addresses.

claim: The SJL mouse EAE model is a model of relapsing/remitting CNS autoimmunity and meningeal inflammation.
source: Here, we present a spatial transcriptomic dataset and analysis in a mouse model of relapsing/remitting CNS autoimmunity and meningeal inflammation, Swiss Jim Lambert (SJL) mouse EAE (Magliozzi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magliozzi et al., 2004 and is a characterization of the model used.

claim: Meningeal areas of gadolinium contrast enhancement on MRI in SJL EAE correspond histologically to collections of B cells, T cells, and myeloid cells.
source: Our prior work in SJL EAE demonstrated meningeal areas of gadolinium contrast enhancement on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that correspond histologically to collections of B cells, T cells, and myeloid cells (Bhargava et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by Bhargava et al., 2021.

claim: In the parenchyma adjacent to areas of meningeal inflammation in SJL EAE, there is astrocytosis, activated microglia, demyelination, and evidence of axonal stress and damage.
source: In the parenchyma adjacent to areas of meningeal inflammation we identified astrocytosis, activated microglia, demyelination, and evidence of axonal stress and damage (Bhargava et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by Bhargava et al., 2021.

claim: Mice developed a characteristic relapsing pattern of neurologic impairment in the SJL EAE model.
source: Mice developed a characteristic relapsing pattern of neurologic impairment, and contrast-enhanced MRI was performed at weeks 6, 8, and 10 post-immunization (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Contrast-enhanced MRI was performed at weeks 6, 8, and 10 post-immunization.
source: Mice developed a characteristic relapsing pattern of neurologic impairment, and contrast-enhanced MRI was performed at weeks 6, 8, and 10 post-immunization (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: In the SJL EAE model, contrast enhancing meningeal lesions are most frequently found in the intrapeduncular cistern, quadrigeminal cistern, and the cleft between the hippocampus and medial geniculate nucleus.
source: In the SJL EAE model, contrast enhancing meningeal lesions are most frequently found in the intrapeduncular cistern, quadrigeminal cistern, and the cleft between the hippocampus and medial geniculate nucleus (Bhargava et al., 2021; Bedussi et al., 2017; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bhargava et al., 2021 and Bedussi et al., 2017, and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Lesion number remained stable throughout the disease course independent of EAE score.
source: Lesion number remained stable throughout the disease course independent of EAE score (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: CFA alone does not produce lasting glial reactivity or LMI formation.
source: Since naïve animals were used as controls, we confirmed that CFA alone does not produce lasting glial reactivity or LMI formation.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: There was no evidence of LMI development in CFA only animals.
source: There was no evidence of LMI development, and no difference in glial reactivity as measured by GFAP, IBA1, or CD68 intensity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: There was no difference in glial reactivity between naïve and CFA only animals as measured by GFAP, IBA1, or CD68 intensity.
source: There was no evidence of LMI development, and no difference in glial reactivity as measured by GFAP, IBA1, or CD68 intensity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Spatial transcriptomic data from all samples were of high quality and read depth.
source: Spatial transcriptomic data from all samples were of high quality and read depth when assessed by treatment group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C) or sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by quality control metrics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E.

claim: There was expected anatomic variability in number of read counts and number of features per spot, with relatively low counts and features in white matter as compared to the cortex or hippocampus.
source: There was expected anatomic variability in number of read counts and number of features per spot, with relatively low counts and features in white matter as compared to the cortex or hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G), and spots had similar degrees of average complexity between EAE and naïve samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by spatial feature plots shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: Spots had similar degrees of average complexity between EAE and naïve samples.
source: There was expected anatomic variability in number of read counts and number of features per spot, with relatively low counts and features in white matter as compared to the cortex or hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G), and spots had similar degrees of average complexity between EAE and naïve samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claim: UMAP clustering revealed no significant independent effect of sample or slide.
source: UMAP clustering revealed no significant independent effect of sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I) or slide (Figure 1—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This is supported by UMAP plots shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I and J.

claim: Numerous genes were differentially expressed between EAE and naïve slices.
source: Numerous genes were differentially expressed between EAE and naïve slices as estimated by DESeq2 on samples pseudobulked by biological replicate (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2K), including genes associated with the complement cascade, immune infiltration, antigen presentation, and astrocyte activation (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2L).
evidence: This is supported by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2K and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Genes associated with the complement cascade, immune infiltration, antigen presentation, and astrocyte activation were differentially expressed between EAE and naïve slices.
source: Numerous genes were differentially expressed between EAE and naïve slices as estimated by DESeq2 on samples pseudobulked by biological replicate (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2K), including genes associated with the complement cascade, immune infiltration, antigen presentation, and astrocyte activation (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2L).
evidence: This is supported by spatial feature plots in Figure 1F and expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2L.

claim: Inflammatory pathways related to TNF, JAK-STAT, and NFκB signaling were upregulated in EAE compared to naïve.
source: Inflammatory pathways related to TNF, JAK-STAT, and NFκB signaling were upregulated in EAE compared to naïve, with peak activity around sites of meningeal inflammation (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by PROGENy pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: TNF, JAK-STAT, and NFκB signaling pathways show peak activity around sites of meningeal inflammation.
source: Inflammatory pathways related to TNF, JAK-STAT, and NFκB signaling were upregulated in EAE compared to naïve, with peak activity around sites of meningeal inflammation (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by spatial plots of pathway activity shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pathways related to Trail and PI3K were downregulated in EAE compared to naïve.
source: Pathways related to Trail and PI3K were downregulated in EAE compared to naïve (Figure 2D and E), and TGFβ pathway activity was unchanged between groups (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by PROGENy pathway analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: TGFβ pathway activity was unchanged between EAE and naïve groups.
source: Pathways related to Trail and PI3K were downregulated in EAE compared to naïve (Figure 2D and E), and TGFβ pathway activity was unchanged between groups (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by PROGENy pathway analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Unbiased UMAP clustering identified 12 distinct clusters in the spatial transcriptomic dataset.
source: To focus our analyses on foci of meningeal inflammation specifically, we performed unbiased UMAP clustering on the spatial transcriptomic dataset and identified 12 distinct clusters (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP plot shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cluster eleven (C11) was restricted to EAE samples.
source: Grouping the dimensional reduction UMAP plot by EAE and naïve revealed that cluster eleven (C11) was restricted to EAE samples (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP plot shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C11 makes up 1–5% of the total spots in EAE samples.
source: C11 makes up 1–5% of the total spots in those samples (Figure 3C), or about 20–120 total spots, and was significantly enriched in EAE relative to naïve samples (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the bar plot shown in Figure 3C.

claim: C11 was significantly enriched in EAE relative to naïve samples.
source: C11 makes up 1–5% of the total spots in those samples (Figure 3C), or about 20–120 total spots, and was significantly enriched in EAE relative to naïve samples (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 3D.

claim: C11 overlaps with areas of meningeal MRI enhancement.
source: Visualizing the clusters using spatial feature plots confirmed that most clusters map consistently to specific anatomic regions and were similar between naïve and EAE (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). C11 overlapped with previously noted areas of meningeal MRI enhancement, suggesting that C11 represents areas of meningeal inflammation (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B—D).
evidence: This is supported by spatial feature plots and MRI correlation shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: C11 represents areas of meningeal inflammation.
source: C11 overlapped with previously noted areas of meningeal MRI enhancement, suggesting that C11 represents areas of meningeal inflammation (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B—D).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial overlap between C11 and MRI-identified meningeal inflammation.

claim: 132 genes were upregulated and 70 genes were downregulated in C11 compared to other clusters.
source: We compared the gene expression in C11 to other clusters and found 132 upregulated genes and 70 downregulated genes (p<0.05; log 2 fold change >1; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Inflammation-related genes were prominently represented in C11 relative to other clusters.
source: Inflammation-related genes were prominently represented in C11 relative to other clusters (Supplementary file 2), with top genes including Cd74, C3, and Gfap (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3G and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Top genes enriched in C11 include Cd74, C3, and Gfap.
source: Inflammation-related genes were prominently represented in C11 relative to other clusters (Supplementary file 2), with top genes including Cd74, C3, and Gfap (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The presence of glial genes such as Gfap within cluster 11 likely represents areas of sub-pial brain parenchyma included within the cluster.
source: The presence of glial genes such as Gfap within cluster 11 likely represents areas of sub-pial brain parenchyma included within the cluster.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the spatial resolution limitations of the method.

claim: Immunoglobulin genes were upregulated in C11.
source: Immunoglobulin genes, which are highly expressed in areas of human GMP (Magliozzi et al., 2019), were also upregulated in C11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Immunoglobulin genes are highly expressed in areas of human gray matter pathology.
source: Immunoglobulin genes, which are highly expressed in areas of human GMP (Magliozzi et al., 2019), were also upregulated in C11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magliozzi et al., 2019.

claim: 538 variable gene sets were identified in C11 spots using gene ontology database analysis.
source: We next performed gene set enrichment analysis of C11 spots using the gene ontology (GO) database (Carbon et al., 2021; Ashburner et al., 2000), finding 538 variable gene sets (adjusted p-value<0.05; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis detailed in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Gene sets involved in antigen processing and presentation, complement activation, lymphocyte activation, and cytokine production and response were prominently enriched in C11.
source: Among the most prominently enriched gene sets were those involved in antigen processing and presentation, complement activation, lymphocyte activation, and cytokine production and response (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Unbiased subclustering identified EAE-specific subclusters within clusters 1 and 2.
source: We performed unbiased subclustering of each cluster in turn and found EAE-specific subclusters and differentially expressed genes within clusters 1 and 2. These subclusters were labeled 1_3, 1_4, and 2_6 (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and represent regions of the thalamus and hypothalamus (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by subclustering analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Subclusters 1_3, 1_4, and 2_6 represent regions of the thalamus and hypothalamus.
source: We performed unbiased subclustering of each cluster in turn and found EAE-specific subclusters and differentially expressed genes within clusters 1 and 2. These subclusters were labeled 1_3, 1_4, and 2_6 (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and represent regions of the thalamus and hypothalamus (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by spatial feature plots shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In subclusters of cluster 2, the EAE-specific subcluster was significantly closer to C11 on average compared to other subclusters.
source: In the subclusters of cluster 1, we found no difference in proximity to C11 between EAE-specific subclusters vs. subclusters present in EAE and naïve. However, in subclusters of cluster 2, the EAE-specific subcluster was significantly closer to C11 on average compared to other subclusters (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All EAE-specific subclusters displayed enrichment of GO gene sets related to inflammation, antigen processing and presentation, and humoral immunity.
source: To explore which pathways were activated in these subclusters, we performed gene set enrichment analysis using the GO database (Figure 4E–G; Supplementary file 4, Supplementary file 5, Supplementary file 6). All subclusters displayed enrichment of GO gene sets related to inflammation, antigen processing and presentation, and humoral immunity.
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: Pathways related to neuron death, cellular stress, and negative regulation of cellular processes were enriched in EAE-specific subclusters.
source: Interestingly, pathways related to neuron death, cellular stress, and negative regulation of cellular processes were also enriched (Figure 4E–G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pathways related to positive regulation of apoptotic process or programmed cell death were upregulated in subcluster 1_3 but downregulated in subcluster 1_4.
source: Interestingly, other pathways related to cell death, including positive regulation of apoptotic process or programmed cell death, were upregulated in subcluster 1_3 but downregulated in subcluster 1_4, suggesting spatially variable survival signals (Supplementary file 4, Supplementary file 5, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis detailed in Supplementary files 4, 5, and 6.

claim: 31 upregulated pathways were conserved between cluster 11 and subclusters 1_3, 1_4, 2_6.
source: Overall, 31 upregulated pathways were conserved between cluster 11 and subclusters 1_3, 1_4, 2_6 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Conserved upregulated pathways between cluster 11 and EAE-specific subclusters include those related to adaptive/B-cell-mediated immunity, antigen processing and presentation, and cell killing.
source: We found prominent conserved upregulation of pathways related to adaptive/B-cell-mediated immunity, antigen processing and presentation, cell killing, and others (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Inflammatory signals increased in meningeal inflammation have variable 'penetration' into the adjacent brain.
source: Our pathway analysis of meningeal inflammation and areas of inflamed adjacent brain parenchyma suggested that inflammatory signals increased in meningeal inflammation could have variable 'penetration' into the adjacent brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the pathway analysis and subclustering results.

claim: Gene sets related to antigen processing and presentation, cell killing, IL-6 production, and IFNγ response have the best fit to a gradient descending pattern of expression along trajectories from meningeal inflammation into brain parenchyma.
source: There was variability in fit to the gradient descending pattern of expression, representing a more gradual decline in pathway enrichment along the trajectory, with gene sets related to antigen processing and presentation, cell killing, IL-6 production, and IFNγ response having the best fit (Figure 5Fi).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5Fi.

claim: C3 expression declines rapidly along the trajectory from meningeal inflammation into brain parenchyma.
source: C3 expression declines rapidly along the trajectory and the logarithmic descending residual AUC is lower than gradient descending residual AUC (Figure 5E), while B2m follows a less steep decline and fits the two patterns similarly (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: B2m follows a less steep decline along the trajectory from meningeal inflammation into brain parenchyma compared to C3.
source: C3 expression declines rapidly along the trajectory and the logarithmic descending residual AUC is lower than gradient descending residual AUC (Figure 5E), while B2m follows a less steep decline and fits the two patterns similarly (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Fcgr3, B2m, Cd74, Gfap, and C3 transcripts were substantially induced in EAE as compared to naïve.
source: We next validated this variability in pattern of expression in a separate cohort of SJL mice with EAE using RNAscope to label selected transcripts related to glial activation (Fcgr3 and Gfap) antigen presentation (B2m and Cd74) and complement (C3) (Figure 5G and I). Consistent with our spatial transcriptomics data, each of these transcripts was substantially induced in EAE as compared to naïve (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope validation shown in Figure 5G, I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For all validated transcripts, the number of positive cells decreased with distance from leptomeningeal inflammation exponentially.
source: We quantified the shortest distance of each target-positive cell from the region of LMI (Figure 5H and J). For all transcripts, the number of positive cells decreased with distance exponentially.
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope quantification shown in Figure 5H and J.

claim: C3 has a higher rate of decrement with distance from leptomeningeal inflammation compared to B2m.
source: The exponential constant b reflects the rate of decrement and had higher absolute value in C3 (b=–1.13) relative to B2m (b=–0.59) (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by exponential regression analysis detailed in Supplementary file 7.

claim: Meninges-restricted inflammation in MS is intimately related to sub-pial gray matter demyelination.
source: Meninges-restricted inflammation in MS is intimately related to sub-pial gray matter demyelination (Howell et al., 2011), atrophy, and neurocognitive symptoms, but therapeutically targeting this aspect of the disease is challenging due to poorly understood pathologic mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Howell et al., 2011.

claim: Therapeutically targeting meninges-restricted inflammation is challenging due to poorly understood pathologic mechanisms.
source: Meninges-restricted inflammation in MS is intimately related to sub-pial gray matter demyelination (Howell et al., 2011), atrophy, and neurocognitive symptoms, but therapeutically targeting this aspect of the disease is challenging due to poorly understood pathologic mechanisms.
evidence: This identifies a clinical challenge that motivates the research.

claim: Each spot in the spatial transcriptomics method used is approximately 55 µm in diameter.
source: An important limitation of the spatial transcriptomics method used in this study is the spatial resolution of each spot. Since each spot is ~55 µm in diameter it is likely that multiple cells are captured in each one.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the 10x Visium platform used.

claim: Multiple cells are likely captured in each spot of the spatial transcriptomics method used.
source: An important limitation of the spatial transcriptomics method used in this study is the spatial resolution of each spot. Since each spot is ~55 µm in diameter it is likely that multiple cells are captured in each one.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial resolution of the technology.

claim: Leptomeningeal inflammation in MS is rich in B cells.
source: Prior work supports roles for pathways identified in our dataset, including B cell and IFNγ-mediated responses, in contributing to neurodegeneration in MS. LMI in MS is rich in B cells, and the critical role of B cells in MS has been underscored by the success of B cell depletion in relapsing and progressive MS.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular composition of LMI in MS.

claim: The critical role of B cells in MS has been underscored by the success of B cell depletion in relapsing and progressive MS.
source: LMI in MS is rich in B cells, and the critical role of B cells in MS has been underscored by the success of B cell depletion in relapsing and progressive MS.
evidence: This reflects established clinical knowledge about B cell depletion therapies in MS.

claim: B cell culture supernatants from MS patients, but not healthy controls, are toxic to rat and human neurons and oligodendrocytes.
source: B cell culture supernatants from MS patients, but not healthy controls, are toxic to rat and human neurons and oligodendrocytes with this effect being mediated by the extracellular vesicle fraction of the supernatants (Lisak et al., 2017; Benjamins et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lisak et al., 2017 and Benjamins et al., 2019.

claim: The toxic effect of B cell culture supernatants from MS patients on neurons and oligodendrocytes is mediated by the extracellular vesicle fraction.
source: B cell culture supernatants from MS patients, but not healthy controls, are toxic to rat and human neurons and oligodendrocytes with this effect being mediated by the extracellular vesicle fraction of the supernatants (Lisak et al., 2017; Benjamins et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lisak et al., 2017 and Benjamins et al., 2019.

claim: B cells are sources for inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and GM-CSF.
source: B cells are also sources for inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6 and GM-CSF, and antibodies, which are speculated to contribute to GMP (Bhargava et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bhargava et al., 2022.

claim: The role of IFNγ in the pathogenesis of MS and EAE is complex and likely has stage-specific protective and pathologic effects.
source: The role of IFNγ in the pathogenesis of MS and EAE is complex, and likely has stage-specific protective and pathologic effects (Arellano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arellano et al., 2015.

claim: IFNγ is pathogenic during the initiation phase of EAE but protective later in the course.
source: Its prominent upregulation in EAE was initially considered evidence of its pathogenic nature, but subsequent experiments showed that it was pathogenic during the initiation phase but protective later in the course (Arellano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arellano et al., 2015.

claim: IFNγ signaling and subsequent upregulation of antigen processing and presentation on glia has been identified as a mechanism that could lead to remyelination failure and subsequent neuronal loss.
source: IFNγ signaling and subsequent upregulation of antigen processing and presentation on glia has been identified as a mechanism that could lead to remyelination failure and subsequent neuronal loss (Kirby et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kirby et al., 2019.

claim: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells upregulate antigen presentation and cross-presentation pathways in response to IFNγ, promoting inflammation and making them susceptible to CD8+ T cell killing.
source: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells upregulate antigen presentation and cross-presentation pathways in response to IFNγ, promoting inflammation and making them susceptible to CD8+ T cell killing (Kirby et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kirby et al., 2019.

claim: Upregulation of genes for self-antigen presentation has been noted in neurons and oligodendrocyte lineage cells in post-mortem MS single nucleus RNAseq.
source: Upregulation of genes for self-antigen presentation has also been noted in neurons and oligodendrocyte lineage (OL) cells in post-mortem MS single nucleus RNAseq (Schirmer et al., 2019) and OL cells in EAE (Falcão et al., 2018; Jäkel et al., 2019; Langseth et al., 2023; Kukanja et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schirmer et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2018; Jäkel et al., 2019; Langseth et al., 2023; Kukanja et al., 2024.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics of subcortical white matter lesions from post-mortem MS cases found prominent elevation of TNF signaling.
source: Recent work also assessed subcortical white matter lesions from post-mortem MS cases via spatial transcriptomics, finding prominent elevation of TNF signaling, in agreement with presented results in the SJL EAE model (Lerma-Martin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lerma-Martin et al., 2022.

claim: SJL-EAE does not require pertussis toxin during induction, unlike C57Bl6-EAE.
source: SJL-EAE, unlike the more common C57Bl6-EAE, does not require pertussis toxin during the induction.
evidence: This is a technical detail about the EAE model used.

claim: The majority of LMI identified in mice with SJL EAE occurred in subarachnoid cisterns.
source: While SJL EAE models many features of LMI in MS (Magliozzi et al., 2004), there are important differences that limit the direct translation of these results to MS. The majority of LMI identified in mice with SJL EAE in our experiments occurred in subarachnoid cisterns, and as a result prominently affected areas of deep gray matter including thalamus and hypothalamus as opposed to cortical lesions also seen in MS.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: LMI in SJL EAE prominently affected areas of deep gray matter including thalamus and hypothalamus as opposed to cortical lesions also seen in MS.
source: The majority of LMI identified in mice with SJL EAE in our experiments occurred in subarachnoid cisterns, and as a result prominently affected areas of deep gray matter including thalamus and hypothalamus as opposed to cortical lesions also seen in MS.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and a comparison to human MS.

claim: Neuronal loss in the thalamus and other deep gray nuclei occurs in MS with a similar 'surface-in' gradient of neuronal injury.
source: Notably, neuronal loss in the thalamus and other deep gray nuclei does occur in MS with a similar 'surface-in' gradient of neuronal injury, thought to also be related to toxic CSF-derived factors (Azevedo et al., 2018; Magliozzi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Azevedo et al., 2018 and Magliozzi et al., 2022.

claim: Demyelination, microglia and astrocyte activation, and neuronal loss are evident in the parenchyma adjacent to LMI in SJL EAE.
source: Demyelination, microglia and astrocyte activation, and neuronal loss are evident in the parenchyma adjacent to LMI in SJL EAE (Bhargava et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bhargava et al., 2021 and Gupta et al., 2023.

claim: Novel rodent models of cytokine-mediated LMI have recently been developed, including virus-mediated meningeal overexpression of TNF and IFNγ or sub-arachnoid injection of recombinant lymphotoxin-α.
source: Notably, novel rodent models of cytokine-mediated LMI have recently been developed, including virus-mediated meningeal overexpression of TNF and IFNγ or sub-arachnoid injection of recombinant lymphotoxin-α, were recently developed, and exhibit lymphoid-like structures (James Bates et al., 2022; James et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to James Bates et al., 2022 and James et al., 2020.

claim: Novel rodent models of cytokine-mediated LMI exhibit lymphoid-like structures.
source: Notably, novel rodent models of cytokine-mediated LMI have recently been developed, including virus-mediated meningeal overexpression of TNF and IFNγ or sub-arachnoid injection of recombinant lymphotoxin-α, were recently developed, and exhibit lymphoid-like structures (James Bates et al., 2022; James et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to James Bates et al., 2022 and James et al., 2020.

claim: This work is the first to characterize a mouse model of LMI and gray matter injury using spatial transcriptomics.
source: This work is the first to characterize a mouse model of LMI and gray matter injury using spatial transcriptomics, and in addition to the analysis presented here contributes a publicly available dataset for future research.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: This work contributes a publicly available dataset for future research.
source: This work is the first to characterize a mouse model of LMI and gray matter injury using spatial transcriptomics, and in addition to the analysis presented here contributes a publicly available dataset for future research.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: Recent advances in RNA extraction from formalin fixed paraffin embedded tissues will allow for the use of large banks of historically collected and preserved samples.
source: While access to appropriate samples remains a significant barrier, recent advances in RNA extraction from formalin fixed paraffin embedded tissues (Newton et al., 2020; Gracia Villacampa et al., 2021) will allow for the use of large banks of historically collected and preserved samples and could dramatically improve availability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newton et al., 2020 and Gracia Villacampa et al., 2021.

claim: Female SJL/J mice aged 7–8 weeks were used in all experiments.
source: Female mice aged 7–8 weeks were used in all experiments and were housed in the animal facility for at least 1 week prior to the start of experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Female SJL/J mice were immunized subcutaneously with 100 μg PLP139-151 peptide with complete Freund's adjuvant containing 4 μg/ml Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37RA to induce EAE.
source: Female SJL/J mice were immunized subcutaneously at two sites over the lateral abdomen with 100 μg PLP139-151 peptide with complete Freund's adjuvant containing 4 μg/ml Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37RA (Difco Laboratories).
evidence: This describes the EAE induction protocol used in the study.

claim: A horizontal 11.7 T scanner was used to image the mouse forebrain at weeks 6, 8, and 10 post-immunization.
source: At weeks 6, 8, and 10 post-immunization, a horizontal 11.7 T scanner (Bruker BioSpin) with a triple-axis gradient system (maximum gradient strength = 740 mT/m), 72 mm volume transmit coil, and four-channel receive-only phased array coil was used to image the mouse forebrain.
evidence: This describes the MRI protocol used in the study.

claim: 0.1 ml diluted Magnevist (gadopentetate dimeglumine, 1:10 with PBS) was injected before MRI imaging.
source: Before imaging, 0.1 ml diluted Magnevist (gadopentetate dimeglumine, Bayer HealthCare LLC, 1:10 with PBS) was injected.
evidence: This describes the contrast agent protocol used in the study.

claim: Brain samples were collected at 11 weeks post-immunization for spatial transcriptomics.
source: At 11 weeks' post-immunization, animals were euthanized in CO2 chamber and perfused with cold PBS.
evidence: This describes the timing of tissue collection for spatial transcriptomics.

claim: Brain samples were cut coronally at a thickness of 10 μm and placed on Visium Gene Expression slides.
source: Fresh frozen brain samples were then cut coronally at a thickness of 10 μm and placed on the capture area of Visium Gene Expression slides (v.1; 10x Genomics).
evidence: This describes the tissue preparation protocol for spatial transcriptomics.

claim: SpaceRanger software (v.1.3.1) was used to pre-process the sequencing data, aligning to the mm10-2020A reference transcriptome.
source: SpaceRanger software (v.1.3.1) was used to pre-process the sequencing data, aligning to the mm10-2020A reference transcriptome.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics pipeline used for data processing.

claim: Spots with less than 250 measured genes and less than 500 unique molecular identifiers were filtered out.
source: Spots with less than 250 measured genes and less than 500 unique molecular identifiers were filtered out.
evidence: This describes the quality control filtering applied to the data.

claim: Data normalization and stabilization of sequence depth variance was performed using SCTransform.
source: Data normalization and stabilization of sequence depth variance was performed on each sample using SCTransform with default parameters (Hafemeister and Satija, 2019).
evidence: This describes the normalization method used, supported by a citation to Hafemeister and Satija, 2019.

claim: Differential gene expression between groups was attained using DESeq2 on samples pseudobulked by biological replicate.
source: Differential gene expression between groups was attained using DESeq2 (v.1.38.2) on samples pseudobulked by biological replicate.
evidence: This describes the differential expression analysis method used.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the GO database and the clusterProfiler package.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis and visualization was performed using the GO database (Carbon et al., 2021; Ashburner et al., 2000) and the clusterProfiler package (v.4.6.0) (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the gene set enrichment analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: Estimated signaling pathway activities were calculated using the PROGENy package.
source: Estimated signaling pathway activities were calculated for each spot with the top 500 genes of each pathway on SCTransformed data using the PROGENy package (v.1.20.0) (Schubert et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the pathway analysis method, supported by a citation to Schubert et al., 2018.

claim: Trajectory gene and gene set modeling analysis was performed with the SPATA2 package.
source: Trajectory gene and gene set modeling analysis was performed with the SPATA2 package.
evidence: This describes the trajectory analysis method used.

claim: RNAscope was performed using the Multiplex Fluorescent Reagent Kit v.2.
source: The RNAscope assay was then carried out using the Multiplex Fluorescent Reagent Kit v.2 (Advanced Cell Diagnostics, Cat. No. 323100) per the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This describes the RNAscope validation method used.

claim: All reported p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg method unless otherwise specified.
source: All reported p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg method (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) unless otherwise specified.
evidence: This describes the statistical correction method used, supported by a citation.
